agree.reason: The letter is measured. It accepts the certificate, makes three concrete and reasonable requests and offers to work with management, which gives a defensive manager a path to act, though the TV station threat may make her dig in.

honest.reason: Most claims track the brief. However, 'more than one day in every eight' is only true if the year is counted to mid-November rather than as a full year. 'Five months later' is inferred, not given. The picture of a resident who must be carried goes slightly beyond the facts.

works_the_facts.reason: It turns 41 days into a rate, 74 households into 'two in every three' and the repeated six-to-eight-week promise into five months of delay. These are well chosen, but it never states what happens if nothing changes, for example the outages projected for next year.

right_comparison.reason: It sets the passing certificate against actual availability and shows the delay repeating since June, which gives an accurate picture of the status quo. It does not weigh the $400,000 against anything.

qualification.reason: The requests and the conditional 'if that is so, show us why' have no deadline for a reply and no stated consequence if management misses it, so the manager has nothing dated to check against.

objections.reason: It meets 'we've handled it' head on by explaining what the certificate does and doesn't show. The two-thirds signature figure quietly answers the 'few loud people' view without raising objections the facts already settle.

fit.reason: It is a properly formed open letter of roughly 400 words, signed by the secretary and suitable for a lobby posting and a press release.
